$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 4 \\ 3 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-4\cdot 3 & =0 \\ 4-4\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-12 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda -8 & =0.\end{aligned}

source.question: e-5481
source.value:
Let's start by writing the matrix $A - \lambda I\mathbin{:}$
﻿﻿![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14068962/assets/ca8f02e390e338b62956302ec45ea274ad73a51dafde3fe93b3d1e37dd663699.png)

Now, let's find and solve the characteristic equation $\det(A-\lambda I) = 0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}10-\lambda  & 3 \\ 6 & 7-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )(7-\lambda )-3\cdot 6 & =0 \\ 70-7\lambda -10\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-18 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-17\lambda +52 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{17\pm \sqrt{(-17)^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot 52}}{2\cdot 1} \\  & =\frac{17\pm \sqrt{81}}{2} \\  & =\frac{17\pm 9}{2} \\  & =13,4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda=13$ and $\lambda=4.$

source.value:
Let's start by writing the matrix $B-\lambda I\mathbin{:}$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14068962/assets/fdbcc62870aefab6214b2f24f53e9bc5654e5386639d4bc328dff3769aff2b45.png)

Now, let's find and solve the characteristic equation $\det(B-\lambda I) = 0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-0\cdot 0 & =0 \\ (\lambda -4)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the matrix $B$ has only one eigenvalue $\lambda=4,$ which is a double root of the characteristic equation. 

**Note:** We also say that $\lambda=4$ has an **algebraic multiplicity** of $2.$

source.value:
Let's start by writing the matrix $A - \lambda I \mathbin{:}$
﻿﻿﻿![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14068962/assets/f91e4886c58db10f60fa666a870aed3c2f456b25e6afb560f857e9c36e81217c.png)

Now, let's find and solve the characteristic equation $\det (A - \lambda I) = 0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 0 \\ 9 & -2\sqrt{3}-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(-2\sqrt{3}-\lambda )-9\cdot 0 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)(\lambda +2\sqrt{3}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the eigenvalues $\lambda={\color{red}3}$ and $\lambda={\color{blue}-2\sqrt{3}}.$

If we look again at the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14068962/assets/aa89b93c6fabd2f3dc7063c85e253ded7482018a5f1c6dadedc74964194c5754.png)
we see that the eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal. This is true in general: the eigenvalues of a *triangular* or *diagonal* matrix are *always* given by the entries on the main diagonal!

**Watch out!** For a general matrix (which is neither triangular nor diagonal), this might not be the case!
